extracted.intended_audience: educators, students of education, and philosophers of education
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical and practical principles for designing, judging, and practicing education in a democratic society, emphasizing transmission, communication, the educative environment, balance of formal and informal instruction, and participation in shared activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as social transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is the means of social continuity of life: the transmission of the beliefs, ideals, skills, and practices of the mature members of a group to its immature members so that the group’s characteristic life continues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dewey emphasizes that because individuals are born immature and adults pass away, deliberate education is necessary to reproduce social life. Examples: initiation ceremonies in simpler societies; in complex societies deliberate schooling and materials are needed. Anti-pattern: assuming continuity will occur automatically without intentional transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education requires communication to create common understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Society 'exists in transmission, in communication' — what forms a community are aims, beliefs, aspirations, and knowledge shared by members; communication secures similar emotional and intellectual dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective education makes experiences and meanings common through communicative processes. Guidance stresses that mere physical proximity or coordinated action does not produce community unless participants share purposes and are informed of one another's aims. Example: a book or letter can institute intimate association across distance when it communicates shared meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish training from educative teaching (partner vs. instrumentality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Training modifies outer action and produces habits useful to others; education (true social education) makes the child a sharer or partner in common activities so that ideas and emotions of the group are aroused in him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for good education: the learner participates in shared ends and feels success/failure as shared, rather than merely being manipulated to produce desired acts. Anti-pattern: treating children 'like an animal' to secure useful habits without forming shared interests; training that leaves instincts attached only to original objects of pleasure/pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep balance between incidental (informal) and formal (intentional) education
rubrics_metrics.description: As societies become complex, formal/intended schooling increases, but there must be a proper balance between informal, incidental education gained by living with others and deliberate school instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good educational practice avoids an undesirable split between school-acquired knowledge and knowledge absorbed through life. Danger: formal instruction becoming remote, abstract, 'bookish', producing 'egoistic specialists' or 'sharps' who cannot integrate learning into social disposition. Aim to integrate formal studies with vital experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter and instruction must be connected to life‑experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Material of formal instruction should not be isolated from subject matter of life-experience; otherwise schooling becomes only technical information expressed in symbols and loses permanent social interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: curriculum and lessons should be translatable into meaningful acts and social practices. Examples: when symbolic knowledge (books, signs) is assimilated through vicarious or imaginative shared activity, it acquires meaning. Anti-pattern: teaching as rote manipulation of symbols without imaginative or social anchoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: The environment must be educative (conditions that promote characteristic activities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Environment consists of conditions that promote or hinder, stimulate or inhibit the characteristic activities of a living being; an educative environment calls out responses that form dispositions and habits aligned with social aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design environments (physical, social, curricular) so they sustain desired activities and dispositions. Dewey notes the environment is not merely physical surroundings but those conditions continuous with an individual's active tendencies. Example: arranging tasks and materials to stimulate musical activity in a musical family.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make learners partners in shared activities (engagement & participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The completing step of educative formation is to make the individual a sharer or partner in the associated activity so that he feels its success as his success and its failure as his failure, thereby internalizing the group's ideas and emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical criterion: involve learners directly in cooperative pursuits, games, and practices where they experience shared aims. This principle applies to both overt activities and imaginative participation invoked by language or narratives. Anti-pattern: purely stimulus-response conditioning that never makes the learner a co‑participant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and symbols must be learned through shared use and imaginative participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Words and symbols gain meaning by being used in joint activities; language learning is an extension of the principle that things gain meaning by being used in shared experience and by imaginative rehearsal of activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching language or abstract concepts, connect words to actions or to vivid imaginative participation in the activities they signify. Otherwise words operate merely as physical stimuli without intellectual value. Example: 'hat' gains meaning for a child when uttered in the shared action of putting on a hat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should form mental and emotional dispositions, not only outward habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Education modifies mental and emotional dispositions of behavior by engaging individuals in activities that arouse and strengthen certain impulses and purposes; outer habits alone are insufficient for genuine education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess educational quality by whether learners adopt the group's intellectual-emotional attitudes (interests, ends), not merely perform externally correct acts. Anti-pattern: automatic responses (dodging, rote performance) without corresponding thought or feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design schooling to avoid remoteness and dead abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal instruction easily becomes remote and dead—abstract and bookish—if it is not kept in proper relation to vital social experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for curriculum/methods: preserve personal, vital qualities in instruction; make school material personally meaningful and tied to real interests. Warning: failure here produces a split between consciously learned material and the formation of character through lived intercourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for complexity of modern life by intentional agencies and explicit materials
rubrics_metrics.description: As civilization advances, the gap between capacities of the young and adult concerns widens, creating a need for intentional agencies (schools) and explicit materials (studies) to transmit complex knowledge and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when apprenticeship/play is insufficient and design intentional teaching to give access to symbolic and technical resources. At the same time, ensure such intentional teaching is integrated with practical meaning to avoid the pitfalls of abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate educational practices by their effect on quality of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The worth of any social institution or educational arrangement is its effect in enlarging and improving conscious experience; this effect should be a primary criterion in educational philosophy and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use improvement of quality of experience (intellectual, emotional, moral) as a yardstick for curricula, methods, and institutions. Example: assess whether an association, practice, or course enlarges imagination, responsibility, and understanding, not merely outputs or technical proficiency.
